answer:
`0dp` — in ConstraintLayout that is `MATCH_CONSTRAINT`, "fill exactly the space my start and end constraints leave"; `match_parent` ignores the constraints and takes the parent's width instead.

### The three sizes
- `wrap_content` — as big as the content; constraints only position it. Add `app:layout_constrainedWidth="true"` if you want it to shrink rather than overflow past a constraint.
- `0dp` — measured from the constraints on that axis, and the only size that reacts to a sibling moving. It needs a constraint on *both* sides of that axis, otherwise it collapses to zero and the view disappears.
- `match_parent` — legal, but on a child it is almost always the bug above: it is the parent's size no matter what you constrained it to. Keep it for the root.

`0dp` is also what unlocks the modifiers: `app:layout_constraintDimensionRatio="16:9"` and `app:layout_constraintWidth_percent="0.4"`.

### What replaces nested weights
- A **chain** — two or more views constrained to each other in both directions — is the LinearLayout weight done flat. `layout_constraintHorizontal_chainStyle` (`spread`, `spread_inside`, `packed`) goes on the head of the chain, and `layout_constraintHorizontal_weight` on `0dp` members divides the space.
- A **Guideline** is an invisible fixed or percentage line you constrain against, so two columns need no wrapper.
- A **Barrier** follows whichever of several referenced views is currently widest — the right tool for a label column that changes length when the app is translated.

Rule of thumb: if you are nesting a ConstraintLayout inside a ConstraintLayout to get weights, you want a chain, a Guideline or a Barrier — a flat hierarchy is the entire point of the layout.
code_example:
<!-- WRONG: match_parent ignores the constraints and slides under @id/action -->
<TextView
    android:id="@+id/title"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintEnd_toStartOf="@id/action" />

<!-- RIGHT: 0dp = MATCH_CONSTRAINT — fill exactly what start..end leaves -->
<TextView
    android:id="@+id/title"
    android:layout_width="0dp"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintEnd_toStartOf="@id/action" />

<!-- A chain is the flat replacement for weights: members constrain to each other both ways -->
<Button
    android:id="@+id/cancel"
    android:layout_width="0dp"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    app:layout_constraintHorizontal_chainStyle="spread"
    app:layout_constraintHorizontal_weight="1"
    app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintEnd_toStartOf="@id/confirm" />
<Button
    android:id="@+id/confirm"
    android:layout_width="0dp"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    app:layout_constraintHorizontal_weight="2"
    app:layout_constraintStart_toEndOf="@id/cancel"
    app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent" />

<!-- A Barrier tracks the widest label, so translation cannot break the column -->
<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.Barrier
    android:id="@+id/labelsEnd"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    app:barrierDirection="end"
    app:constraint_referenced_ids="labelName,labelEmail" />

A Fragment outlives its view: after `onDestroyView` the Fragment instance can sit on the back stack for a long time, and a binding field keeps the destroyed view tree — every View, every drawable, every bitmap in it — reachable.

### What ViewBinding generates
For each XML layout it generates one class named from the file (`fragment_profile.xml` → `FragmentProfileBinding`) with a final field per `android:id`, plus `inflate()`, `bind()` and `getRoot()`. Turn it on with `buildFeatures { viewBinding = true }`; no annotation processor, no build slowdown. Views that exist only in some configuration variants come out nullable, and ids from `<include>` are reachable through the included layout's own binding.

- **DataBinding** is the superset with `<layout>` wrappers, expressions and two-way binding. It needs kapt/KSP and is effectively in maintenance mode — new code uses ViewBinding or Compose.
- **Kotlin synthetics** (`kotlin-android-extensions`) were removed in Kotlin 1.8. They resolved ids globally, so a typo could hand you a view from a different layout and crash at runtime.
- `findViewById` still works and is what `bind()` calls; the win is that the compiler, not you, guarantees the id exists and has that type.

### The Fragment rule
Use a nullable backing field and null it in `onDestroyView`, or a delegate that does the same for you. Only touch `binding` between `onCreateView` and `onDestroyView`. The same lifetime rule applies to anything else the view owns: subscribe with `viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope` and `repeatOnLifecycle`, not the Fragment's own `lifecycleScope`, or a collector will keep updating views that no longer exist.

Rule of thumb: in an Activity a binding field is fine, because the Activity and its view die together; in a Fragment it never is.

`dp` scales with screen density only, while `sp` scales with density *and* the user's font-scale setting — so text sized in `dp` silently ignores the accessibility setting, and a box sized in `dp` around `sp` text clips it.

### The three units
- `px` — one physical pixel. Belongs in drawing and measuring code, never in a layout file.
- `dp` — density-independent pixel: `px = dp * DisplayMetrics.density`, where density is 1.0 at 160 dpi, 2.0 at xhdpi, 3.0 at xxhdpi. The ldpi…xxxhdpi buckets only pick which `drawable-*` folder is used; the real density of a device can be any value in between, and the user can change it in Display size.
- `sp` — `dp` multiplied by `fontScale`. Every text size, and nothing else.

### What breaks at 200%
- Fixed `dp` heights on rows, chips and buttons: the text grows, the box does not. Use `wrap_content` with `android:minHeight`.
- `maxLines="1"` with no `ellipsize`, and any layout that assumes one line.
- Hand-rolled conversion. Since Android 14 font scaling is **nonlinear** — already-large text grows proportionally less — so multiplying by `fontScale` yourself gives the wrong number. Ask the framework: `TypedValue.applyDimension`, or `resources.getDimensionPixelSize` on a `<dimen>`, and `TypedValue.deriveDimension` (API 34+) for the inverse.

Test with font size at maximum *and* display size at maximum, which are separate settings and compound.

Rule of thumb: text in `sp`, spacing and sizes in `dp`, `px` only where you touch the canvas — and no dimension is ever computed with a hand-written multiply.

`<include>` inlines another layout file but keeps that file's root ViewGroup; making that root a `<merge>` attaches its children straight to the including parent, so the extra level disappears entirely.

### The four tools
- `<include layout="@layout/view_header" />` — inflated in place, at inflation time, costing exactly what the included file costs. `android:id` and `layout_*` on the include tag override the included root's, but only if you also give it `layout_width` and `layout_height`.
- `<merge>` — a root that is not a View at all. Legal only when the file is always included into a parent that supplies the layout params; the preview needs `tools:parentTag` to know how to arrange the children.
- `<ViewStub>` — a zero-by-zero, invisible, drawing-nothing placeholder. Nothing inside it is inflated until you call `inflate()` or set its visibility; the stub then *replaces itself* in the hierarchy with the real layout, so the reference to the stub is dead afterwards and a second `inflate()` throws. Right for an error panel, an empty state or a rarely opened section.
- `tools:` — `tools:text`, `tools:visibility`, `tools:listitem`, `tools:context`. AAPT strips the whole namespace from the built APK, so it costs nothing at runtime and can never be read by your code.

### Where inflation cost lands
`LayoutInflater` instantiates every tag reflectively and parses its attributes on the main thread, inside `setContentView` or `onCreateView` — on the cold-start path, before the first frame. A few hundred views is tens of milliseconds of it. Flatten with ConstraintLayout, defer the rare branches with `ViewStub`, and confirm with a `Trace.beginSection` around inflation or Layout Inspector's tree depth rather than guessing. `AsyncLayoutInflater` exists but cannot inflate layouts that create a `Handler` or use fragments — flatten first.
code_example:
<!-- res/layout/view_header.xml — <merge> so these two attach to the INCLUDING parent -->
<merge xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"
    tools:parentTag="android.widget.LinearLayout">

  <ImageView
      android:id="@+id/avatar"
      android:layout_width="40dp"
      android:layout_height="40dp"
      tools:src="@drawable/ic_person" />

  <!-- tools: is design-time only; AAPT strips it out of the APK -->
  <TextView
      android:id="@+id/name"
      android:layout_width="wrap_content"
      android:layout_height="wrap_content"
      tools:text="Ada Lovelace" />
</merge>

<!-- res/layout/fragment_orders.xml -->
<LinearLayout
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:orientation="vertical">

  <!-- include keeps the included root — unless that root is <merge> -->
  <include
      android:id="@+id/header"
      layout="@layout/view_header"
      android:layout_width="match_parent"
      android:layout_height="wrap_content" />

  <androidx.recyclerview.widget.RecyclerView
      android:id="@+id/list"
      android:layout_width="match_parent"
      android:layout_height="0dp"
      android:layout_weight="1"
      tools:listitem="@layout/item_order" />

  <!-- Costs one 0x0 placeholder until something goes wrong -->
  <ViewStub
      android:id="@+id/errorStub"
      android:layout="@layout/view_error"
      android:inflatedId="@+id/errorPanel"
      android:layout_width="match_parent"
      android:layout_height="wrap_content" />
</LinearLayout>

<!-- Kotlin: val panel = binding.errorStub.inflate()  // replaces the stub; calling it twice throws -->

A `MeasureSpec` is a single packed `Int` holding a mode plus a size — the parent's constraint on that child for one axis — and the child answers it by calling `setMeasuredDimension`.

### The three passes
1. **Measure.** The parent calls `child.measure(widthSpec, heightSpec)`; the child must call `setMeasuredDimension()` before returning or the framework throws `IllegalStateException`. The modes are `EXACTLY` (the parent decided: `match_parent` or a fixed dp), `AT_MOST` (no more than this: `wrap_content`), and `UNSPECIFIED` (take what you want — a ScrollView measuring its child). Use `resolveSize()` instead of branching on the mode yourself. Measure can run more than once per pass — LinearLayout with weights measures twice — so it must be cheap and free of side effects; nested double-measure is why deep hierarchies get exponentially slow.
2. **Layout.** `onLayout(changed, l, t, r, b)` positions children with `child.layout(...)` using only the sizes from step 1. No measuring, no allocation, and never `requestLayout()` from inside it.
3. **Draw.** `onDraw(canvas)` paints. No allocation here either: it runs for every frame, at 120 Hz on current devices, so a `Paint` or `RectF` created here is garbage collected sixty times a second.

### requestLayout vs invalidate
- `requestLayout()` — "my size may have changed". Walks the flag up to the root and schedules measure + layout + draw for that branch. Expensive.
- `invalidate()` — "my pixels changed, my size did not". Schedules `onDraw` only. A progress value, a colour, a selection ring.

The classic trap is a property setter that calls `requestLayout()` for a change that only repaints, driven from an animator sixty times a second — the profiler then shows measure/layout time nobody can explain.

Rule of thumb: ask "could this change my measured size?" If no, `invalidate()`.

Nothing applies padding for you — `onDraw` hands you the whole `0..width` canvas and you must confine yourself to `paddingLeft..width - paddingRight` — and a View saves state only if it has an `android:id` **and** you override `onSaveInstanceState`.

### Attributes
Declare them in `res/values/attrs.xml` inside `<declare-styleable>`, then read them in the constructor with `context.obtainStyledAttributes(attrs, R.styleable.RatingView, defStyleAttr, 0)`, and recycle the `TypedArray` — `use { }` from core-ktx does it for you. Use `@JvmOverloads constructor(... defStyleAttr: Int = 0)` so the two-argument form XML inflation looks for actually exists.

### Drawing inside the padding
Compute the content box once in `onSizeChanged`, not per frame, and keep `Paint`, `Path` and `RectF` as fields. Honour `paddingStart`/`paddingEnd` rather than left/right if the view must mirror in RTL. If you subclass a `ViewGroup` and want `onDraw` at all, call `setWillNotDraw(false)`.

### Saving your own state
- `onSaveInstanceState()` must call `super.onSaveInstanceState()` and carry that result as the `superState` of a `BaseSavedState` subclass; dropping it loses the base class's state.
- `onRestoreInstanceState` receives your `SavedState` — unwrap it, pass `superState` up, then read your fields. Guard the cast, because a mismatched id can hand you someone else's Parcelable.
- No `android:id`, no saved state. Nor is the id allowed to repeat in the hierarchy: two views with the same id both write into the same slot, which is exactly why a container of repeated rows uses `android:saveEnabled="false"` or `dispatchFreezeSelfOnly()`.

Rule of thumb: attributes in the constructor, geometry in `onSizeChanged`, zero allocation in `onDraw`, and state only ever reaches a View that has an id.

The Adapter owns the data and turns an item into a bound row, the ViewHolder is a cache of `findViewById` results for one reusable row, the LayoutManager decides where rows go and when they stop being visible, and the RecycledViewPool holds the detached holders keyed by view type.

### The division of labour
- `onCreateViewHolder(parent, viewType)` runs only when the pool has nothing of that type to give back. Inflate with `attachToRoot = false` and pass `parent`, so the row gets the LayoutParams the LayoutManager expects. Everything that is per-row-forever — click listeners, a `TextWatcher`, a formatter — is wired here, once.
- `onBindViewHolder(holder, position)` runs every time a row scrolls into view, dozens of times per second while flinging. Its contract is `state = f(item)`: assign **every** field on **every** path, because the holder arrives carrying the previous item's content.
- The LayoutManager — `LinearLayoutManager`, `GridLayoutManager`, `StaggeredGridLayoutManager` — measures and positions children, drives scrolling, and decides which views go to the scrap heap or the pool.
- `RecycledViewPool` — five holders per view type by default (`setMaxRecycledViews` changes it). Two RecyclerViews with identical row types can share one via `setRecycledViewPool`, which is what makes a vertical list of horizontal carousels stop re-inflating.

### What bind must never do
- **Never capture `position`.** It is stale the moment anything is inserted above. Read `holder.bindingAdapterPosition` at click time and bail on `NO_POSITION`.
- **Never create a listener or an object per bind** — that is allocation on the scroll path and a fresh lambda on every row.
- **No I/O, no bitmap decode, no database or `SharedPreferences` read.** Bind runs during layout on the main thread.
- **Never call `notify*` from inside bind.** RecyclerView is mid-layout; it throws or corrupts its own state.

Rule of thumb: create wires it up once, bind is a pure function of the item — and if bind has an `if` without an `else`, you have found your recycling bug.

`notifyDataSetChanged()` declares everything invalid, so RecyclerView rebinds every visible row, runs no item animations and cannot preserve positional state; `ListAdapter` (or `AsyncListDiffer` directly) computes a real diff and emits granular insert, remove, move and change events instead.

### The two callbacks
- `areItemsTheSame(old, new)` — "is this the same entity?" Compare identifiers only. This is what decides move versus remove-plus-insert, and therefore whether a row animates or blinks out of existence.
- `areContentsTheSame(old, new)` — "does it look the same?" Called only for items already judged the same; a `data class` `equals` is usually right, as long as the model is immutable and holds no lambdas.
- Swap them — compare whole objects in `areItemsTheSame` — and every edit becomes a delete plus an insert: the row flashes, loses focus and the list scroll jumps.

### Payloads, threads and stable ids
- `getChangePayload(old, new)` returns a token for a partial change; the three-argument `onBindViewHolder(holder, position, payloads)` then updates just that view and, critically, does **not** cancel the running item animation. If `payloads` is empty, delegate to the full bind.
- `submitList()` runs the diff on a background executor and applies the result on the main thread. Because it is asynchronous, never mutate the list you already submitted — the differ would compare a list against itself and silently drop the update. Submit a new immutable list every time. The `submitList(list) { }` overload gives you a commit callback for scrolling afterwards.
- `setHasStableIds(true)` plus `getItemId` only matters for `notifyDataSetChanged` and cross-adapter reuse; with DiffUtil it is largely redundant, and it is actively harmful if the ids are not genuinely stable.

Rule of thumb: immutable model, a new list into `submitList`, ids answer `areItemsTheSame`, `equals` answers `areContentsTheSame`.

All three are one bug in three costumes: a ViewHolder is a view that gets reused, so its old state survives, and `onBindViewHolder` has to overwrite everything and cancel everything.

### The stale photo
- The image load is asynchronous. The row scrolls away and is rebound before the old request finishes, and that request still points at the same `ImageView`. Coil's `ImageView.load()` and `Glide.with(imageView)` both cancel the in-flight request for that target, so the plain path is safe — a hand-rolled coroutine or a custom `Target` is not, and has to be cancelled in `onViewRecycled`.
- Cancelling still leaves the previous bitmap on screen until the new one arrives. Set a `placeholder`, or clear the drawable at the top of bind.

### The wrong checkbox
- Bind must be total: every view gets a value on every bind, with no branch that assigns a field only sometimes. A field set inside an `if` is showing some other row's value the rest of the time.
- The listener trap — `setOnCheckedChangeListener` fires when bind itself writes `isChecked`, so the row reports the previous item's state as a user toggle. Detach the listener, set the value, reattach.
- Never capture `position` in a click lambda. Read `bindingAdapterPosition` inside the callback and bail on `NO_POSITION`; the captured one is stale the moment a row above is removed.

### The leftover animation
- `alpha`, `translationX` and a running `ViewPropertyAnimator` belong to the view, not to the item, so a holder recycled mid-animation arrives half-transparent. Cancel and reset in `onViewRecycled`, and let `ItemAnimator` own enter and exit animations instead of starting them in bind.

The mental model: `onCreateViewHolder` builds, `onBindViewHolder` overwrites. If a property is only assigned on one path, sooner or later a user sees someone else's data.

Let the model carry the type — `getItemViewType` becomes an exhaustive `when` over a sealed row type — and let `ConcatAdapter` hold the header and the footer as separate adapters, so no offset ever enters the arithmetic.

### One adapter, a sealed list
- Model the screen as `List<Row>` where `Row` is a sealed interface. `getItemViewType(position)` is a `when` over that type, so adding a row kind is a compile error in one place instead of a silent `IndexOutOfBoundsException` in another.
- The `Int` you return is opaque to RecyclerView: it only picks a slot in the `RecycledViewPool` and comes back as the `viewType` argument of `onCreateViewHolder`. A layout id is a convenient unique constant.
- With `ListAdapter`, `areItemsTheSame` sees both types on both sides, so compare the class first and the id second — an `Ad` with id 7 is not the `Article` with id 7.

### Headers and footers: ConcatAdapter
- `ConcatAdapter(headerAdapter, feedAdapter, loadMoreAdapter)` presents several adapters as one list. Each keeps its own positions and its own `submitList`, so adding a header never shifts the diff of the list under it.
- Inside a child adapter, `bindingAdapterPosition` is the local position and `absoluteAdapterPosition` is the position in the whole concatenation. Picking the wrong one is the modern version of the same off-by-one.
- `ConcatAdapter.Config` isolates view types per child by default; turn that off only when two children genuinely want to share a pool.

### Why the arithmetic rots
`position - 1` hard-codes "there is exactly one header" into every method of the adapter. The day the banner becomes conditional, the diff, the click handler and the item decoration each disagree about the offset — three separate bugs, and only one of them crashes loudly.

A touch walks down the tree through `dispatchTouchEvent`, giving every parent a veto in `onInterceptTouchEvent` on the way down and every child a chance to consume in `onTouchEvent` on the way back up — and whoever consumes `ACTION_DOWN` owns the rest of that gesture.

### The walk
1. `Activity.dispatchTouchEvent` hands the event to the window, the DecorView, and then each `ViewGroup.dispatchTouchEvent` in turn.
2. Before passing it to a child, the group calls its own `onInterceptTouchEvent`. Returning `true` takes the gesture: the child that had it receives a single `ACTION_CANCEL` and nothing after.
3. Otherwise the child sees it — `OnTouchListener` first, then `onTouchEvent`. A view that returns `false` for `ACTION_DOWN` is out of the whole gesture: no MOVE, no UP.
4. Anything unconsumed bubbles back up through the parents' `onTouchEvent`.

### Deciding instead of fighting
- Intercept on distance, never on DOWN. Record the down point and steal only once movement passes `ViewConfiguration.get(context).scaledTouchSlop` **along your own axis**. That is exactly why two RecyclerViews of opposite orientation already coexist with no code from you.
- A child that knows the gesture is its own calls `parent.requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(true)`. The framework clears that flag on the next `ACTION_DOWN`, so it is a per-gesture call, not something you set once in `init`.
- Same-orientation nesting is the case that genuinely breaks — a horizontal RecyclerView inside a `ViewPager2`. The fix is a wrapper that disallows interception only while the child can still scroll that way, which is what `NestedScrollableHost` in the ViewPager2 samples does.

And never put a RecyclerView inside a `ScrollView` to dodge a layout problem: it measures every row, recycling is gone, and the gesture conflict is the least expensive symptom.

Spacing and dividers are properties of the list, not of the row, so they belong in an `ItemDecoration`; the swipe is a gesture over the list, so it belongs in an `ItemTouchHelper` — and neither one needs the adapter to know about it.

### ItemDecoration: three hooks
- `getItemOffsets` reserves space around a child. The LayoutManager adds it to the child's bounds, so it acts like a margin the row never declared — this is where grid gutters and "no gap after the last row" live.
- `onDraw` paints under the items and `onDrawOver` paints on top of them: dividers below, sticky headers and swipe backgrounds above.
- Ready-made: `DividerItemDecoration(context, LinearLayoutManager.VERTICAL)`, with `setDrawable` if the default line is wrong.
- The traps: it runs for every child on every layout pass, so allocate nothing inside it; call `addItemDecoration` once, because a second call stacks another set of offsets; and resolve positions with `parent.getChildAdapterPosition(view)`, guarding `NO_POSITION`.

### ItemTouchHelper: drag and swipe
- `ItemTouchHelper(callback).attachToRecyclerView(list)`, where `SimpleCallback(dragDirs, swipeDirs)` gives you `onMove` and `onSwiped`.
- `onMove` has to reorder your own data and call `notifyItemMoved`. With a `ListAdapter` the smooth path is to move within a working copy on each step and persist once in `clearView` — a `submitList` per move fights the drag it is animating.
- The red background and the trash icon are yours to draw in `onChildDraw`, from `dX` and `isCurrentlyActive`; out of the box the row just translates over nothing.
- It is touch-only. TalkBack cannot swipe, so mirror the action with `ViewCompat.addAccessibilityAction` or an overflow item, or the feature does not exist for those users.

Rule of thumb: if deleting the widget from the row layout would not change what the row *is*, it is decoration — put it on the list.

Nested scrolling is a cooperation protocol: before a scrolling child moves a single pixel it offers the delta to its parents, and `CoordinatorLayout` uses that first refusal to collapse the `AppBarLayout`. A plain `ScrollView` never implements the child half, so nothing is ever offered.

### The handshake, in order
1. On touch down the child calls `startNestedScroll(axes, type)`. Parents that return `true` from `onStartNestedScroll` join the scroll and get `onNestedScrollAccepted`.
2. On every move the child calls `dispatchNestedPreScroll(dx, dy, consumed, offset, type)` first. The parent's `onNestedPreScroll` runs before the child scrolls and takes what it wants — that is the app bar collapsing while the list has not moved at all.
3. The child then scrolls with the remainder and reports both numbers through `dispatchNestedScroll` → `onNestedScroll`, where the parent may consume the leftover. That is the app bar expanding once the list is already at the top.
4. Flings mirror it with `dispatchNestedPreFling` and `dispatchNestedFling`. The `type` argument separates `TYPE_TOUCH` from `TYPE_NON_TOUCH`, the settling phase after the finger is gone.

### What plugs into it
- Child side: `RecyclerView`, `NestedScrollView`, `ViewPager2`, via `NestedScrollingChild3` and usually `NestedScrollingChildHelper`. `ScrollView` and `ListView` implement none of it.
- Parent side: `CoordinatorLayout` forwards each callback above to the `Behavior` of the child named by `app:layout_behavior`. `AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior` — the `@string/appbar_scrolling_view_behavior` you paste onto the list — is what offsets the list below the bar and feeds it those scrolls.
- Inside the `AppBarLayout`, `app:layout_scrollFlags` picks the choreography: `scroll`, `enterAlways`, `exitUntilCollapsed`, `snap`.

### Where it breaks
`android:nestedScrollingEnabled="false"` stops the offers, and a `wrap_content` RecyclerView inside a `NestedScrollView` measures every row and hands scrolling to the parent — one kills the app bar, the other kills recycling with it.

You read a trace instead of guessing: RecyclerView emits its own slices — `RV CreateView`, `RV OnBindView`, `RV Scroll`, `RV Prefetch` — and whichever one is fat on the janky frames tells you which fix is the right one.

### Reading it
- Record with system tracing or a Macrobenchmark scroll run and open it in Perfetto, then line the long frames on the main thread up with those slices.
- Fat `RV CreateView` means inflation: too many view types, or a row hierarchy deep enough that inflate plus measure costs milliseconds. Flatten it into one `ConstraintLayout`, cut view types, and give nested lists a shared `RecycledViewPool` so every row stops inflating its own children.
- Fat `RV OnBindView` means work in bind: bitmap decoding, `SimpleDateFormat`, string building, sorting, a database read. Bind should assign already-formatted fields and nothing else — do the formatting in the ViewModel, off the main thread.
- Neither one fat, frames still long: look under the list. Overdraw from a window background behind an opaque list, a software layer, a large shadow or blur, or a `notifyDataSetChanged` rebinding everything where `DiffUtil` would have touched one row.

### The flags people cargo-cult
- `setHasFixedSize(true)` only asserts that the RecyclerView's own bounds never change when the adapter's contents change, which lets it skip a full layout pass on item updates. It does nothing for bind cost, and nothing at all for a `wrap_content` list.
- Prefetch is already on: `GapWorker` creates and binds the upcoming item in the UI thread's idle slice. What you may have to set is `initialPrefetchItemCount` on the inner `LinearLayoutManager` of a horizontal row, so a carousel prefetches the items that will actually be visible.
- `setItemViewCacheSize` and `RecycledViewPool.setMaxRecycledViews` trade memory for fewer rebinds; they help a list with several expensive view types and hide nothing else.

Measure on a mid-range device in a release build — a debuggable build inflates every number you are about to act on.

Translation, scale, rotation and alpha are RenderNode properties the render thread can re-composite without redrawing anything, while a height change invalidates layout and forces a measure and layout pass over that whole branch on every single frame.

### The three APIs
- `View.animate()` (`ViewPropertyAnimator`) is the default for moving, fading and scaling. It batches every property you set into one animation with a single invalidate per frame, and `withLayer()` puts the view on a hardware layer for the duration and takes it off at the end.
- `ObjectAnimator` / `ValueAnimator` is for what `ViewPropertyAnimator` has no setter for: a colour through `ofArgb`, a custom `Property`, a repeating or reversible animation, or an `AnimatorSet` choreographing several. Prefer a typed property such as `View.TRANSLATION_Y` over a property-name string, which is resolved by reflection.
- `MotionLayout` is a `ConstraintLayout` that interpolates between two `ConstraintSet`s described in a `MotionScene`, and can be driven by a drag through `onSwipe`. It is for choreographing a whole screen, and it does pay for layout work per frame — that is the price of what it buys.

### Layers, and the size trap
- `setLayerType(LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE, null)` renders the view once into a GPU texture, after which transform and alpha cost a re-composite instead of a redraw. Left on permanently it costs texture memory and re-uploads on every content change, so turn it on for the animation and off afterwards — exactly what `withLayer()` does for you.
- When the size change has to be real, hand it to `TransitionManager.beginDelayedTransition(container, ChangeBounds())`: it captures the before and after states and interpolates the bounds, instead of you calling `requestLayout()` sixty times a second. Where a fake will do, `scaleY` with a pivot or a clip costs nothing.

The mental model: if the property you are animating can move your neighbours, you are buying a layout pass every frame.

Android 15 draws every app targeting SDK 35 edge-to-edge whether it asked or not, so the window no longer pads itself: you read `WindowInsetsCompat` and apply the insets yourself, to the specific views that need them.

### What changed
- `enableEdgeToEdge()` from `androidx.activity` is how you opt in on older releases; from API 35 it is the behaviour with or without the call.
- `Window.setStatusBarColor`, `setNavigationBarColor` and the matching theme attributes are deprecated and ignored for apps targeting 35+. Icon contrast is now yours: `WindowCompat.getInsetsController(window, window.decorView).isAppearanceLightStatusBars = true`, or draw your own scrim.
- The opt-out attribute `windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement` is an Android 15 stopgap; it is ignored once you target API 36, so treat it as a deadline, not a fix.

### Applying insets
- `ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener(view) { v, insets -> ... }`, reading `insets.getInsets(Type.systemBars() or Type.displayCutout())`. Return `insets` so siblings still see them — returning `WindowInsetsCompat.CONSUMED` at the root is the classic bug that leaves everything else unpadded.
- Pad the right views for the right reason: the toolbar takes the top inset; the list takes the bottom inset as padding with `android:clipToPadding="false"`, so rows scroll under the navigation bar but the last one still stops above it.
- `android:fitsSystemWindows="true"` still works and still consumes — it pads one view with all the insets and gives its children none. Fine for a single root, wrong the moment two views need different insets, except inside `CoordinatorLayout`, whose Behaviors read the flag deliberately.

### The keyboard
Keep `android:windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize"`, but edge-to-edge means the resize no longer reaches your padding on its own: apply `Type.ime()`. The usual expression is `max(ime.bottom, systemBars.bottom)` as bottom padding, so the layout follows the keyboard when it is open and the navigation bar when it is not. To move in step with the keyboard rather than jumping to its end state, implement `WindowInsetsAnimationCompat.Callback`.
